sections.html:
• Common names: Miami Cave Crayfish, Cave crayfish, Tangerine crayfish
  • Tank size (optimal): 40 litres
  • Breeding: easy
  • Diet: omnivore / carnivore
  • Temperament: conditionally peaceful
  • Life span: up to 4 years
  • Colour form: yellow to red
Procambarus milleri is only known from two localities in Dade County, Florida. This species is endemic to these places.

These crayfish are groundwater animals. They inhabit deep geological formations, greater than 5 m beneath the Rocky Glades, with voids of various dimensions that flood periodically but always contain water.

Researchers stated that virtually nothing is known about this species' natural life traits. Much of what is currently known about the species is based on aquarium observations.

These crayfish are classified as opportunistic omnivores, which means they will eat just about any food they find on the bottom of the tank.

Nonetheless, observations indicated a strong preference for high-protein food. For the best growth, feeds should contain protein at a level of at least 30–40 % of the diet.

Juveniles and pre-adults tended to eat more and show more interest in plant materials than adults. This does not mean they should not be given high-protein food; young simply eat a lot because they grow very fast.

Suggested foods include:

  • leaves
  • plants
  • vegetables
  • crushed snails
  • earthworms
  • live bloodworms
  • frozen bloodworms
  • black worms
  • dead fish or shrimp
  • Artemia
  • fish food (pellets, granules, flakes)
  • shrimp food (Hikari crustacean, algae wafers), etc.

Food should sink to the bottom and should not be too small, otherwise it will be difficult to pick up.

  • Diet type: omnivore / carnivore
  • Food preference: mix of meat and vegetation
  • Feeding frequency: 3–4 times a week for adults, daily for juveniles

Feeding rules

  • Leave their food for 12–24 hours before removing it. Leaves can be left in the tank for several days. Make sure that whatever they do not consume in one day is removed to prevent water contamination.
  • Check the burrows. Crayfish often drag and store food in their hiding spots for later consumption. Check them from time to time to prevent bacterial contamination.
  • Diversity. Do not give them the same food all the time. Provide various food items to diversify the diet, which makes them stronger and helps them grow faster.
  • Aggression. They become more aggressive when hungry. Protein plays a fundamental role in their life; if they do not get enough they become aggressive and may even turn cannibalistic.
  • Calcium also plays a huge role in crayfish.

Fully grown Procambarus milleri is one of the few types of crayfish that can be kept in a community tank relatively safely. They are not as aggressive as their bigger cousins (Blue crayfish, Red crayfish, Marbled crayfish, Cherax destructor, etc.). It is recommended to keep one male and one or two females in the group.

This does not mean that they are social. They just tolerate high stocking densities better than most crayfish species.

Interestingly, these crayfish are the most aggressive when they are young (2.5–7 cm long). Unlike adults, they display strong competition for resources.

Although these crayfish are perceived to be nocturnal because their peak activity is after dusk, they are not timid animals. On the contrary, they are pretty active and outgoing. You will often see them crawling or sitting in the open.

Miami Cave Crayfish cannot be categorized as a primary burrower.

In the aquarium, they also like to move objects around. Overall, they can be pretty messy and destructive.

  • Social: No
  • Active: Yes
  • Peaceful: generally yes (adults), no (juveniles)
  • Burrowers: no (generally)

Description

Miami Cave Crayfish are relatively small but grow really fast. Generally, they grow only up to 8–10 cm long.

These crayfish are available in bright-coloured morphs (yellow or red to yellow) that are dramatically different from their normal wild-type coloration (mostly white with a little bit of yellow).

This mutation comes from the crayfish being bred in captivity and not in the wild. There is no information on who, how, when, and where their yellow colour morph originated for the first time.

Difference between Procambarus milleri, Procambarus alleni and Procambarus clarkii

It can be really hard to tell them apart when they are young. Basically, these species are almost identical in everything.

Procambarus milleri is a very young species. Scientists suggest that it was derived from a parental stock of Procambarus alleni and evolved after the aquifer was lowered in south Florida in the 1920s.

The difference can only be seen once they are fully grown:

  • Size: Procambarus milleri is the smallest one.
  • Temper: Procambarus milleri is the least aggressive.

Lifespan

Currently, there is no data available on the maximum lifespan of Procambarus milleri in the wild. In captivity, these crayfish can live up to 3–4 years if appropriately cared for.
